# The functional importance of the N-terminal region of human Prolylcarboxypeptidase

**Authors:** J Mallela; R Perkins; J Yang; S Pedigo; J Rimoldi; Z Shariat-Madar

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Pharmacology, University of Mississippi, University, MS 38677-1848 | 2 Research Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Mississippi, University, MS 38677-1848 | 3 Department of Chemistry & Biochemistry, University of Mississippi, University, MS 38677-1848 | 4 Department of Medicinal Chemistry, University of Mississippi, University, MS 38677-1848

## Abstract

The renin-angiotensin-system cascade pathway generates the vasopressor and prothrombotic hormones, angiotensin II (Ang II) and angiotensin III (Ang III) from angiotensinogen. One of the key enzymes for the generation of angiotensin 1–7 (Ang 1–7) and angiotensin 2–7 (Ang 2–7) from Ang II and III respectively, is prolylcarboxypeptidase (PRCP). To understand the contribution of the N-terminal region to catalysis, an N-terminal truncated form, lacking 179 N-terminal residues of PRCP (rPRCP40) were constructed. The circular dichroism (CD) spectrum of rPRCP40 illustrated that it was structured with significant helical content as indicated by local minima at ~220 and 208 nm. The main products of Ang III metabolized by rPRCP40 were Ang 2–7 plus phenylalanine as determined by LC-MS. Angiotensin I (Ang I) blocked the metabolism of Ang III by rPRCP40. These investigations showed that the C-terminal region of the rPRCP40 contributes to PRCP’s catalytic function, and provided additional experimental evidence for this suggestion.

## INTRODUCTION

The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) regulates blood pressure, water and electrolyte balance [1;2]. The RAS has been implicated as a major effector of hypertension and other cardiovascular diseases arising from its production of angiotensin II (Ang II) and angiotensin III (Ang III) [3]. Angiotensin II can be metabolized by at least 13 proteases, among which are angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) and prolylcarboxypeptidase (PRCP) which convert Ang II to angiotensin 1–7 (Ang 1–7) [4]. ACE2 and PRCP are switches that transform this peptide from a vasoconstrictor to a vasodilator. Ang (1–7) may act in a synergistic manner to modulate bradykinin-induced vasodilation at the local level. In doing so, ACE2 and PRCP regulate the blood flow through active tissues in order to preserve the internal environment [5]. Thus, ACE2 and PRCP have cardiovascular protective roles [6].

Recently, we found that when the complex of high molecular weight kininogen (HK) and prekallikrein (PK) binds to endothelial cells membranes, PK is rapidly converted to kallikrein by PRCP. Kallikrein then cleaves HK to liberate bradykinin (BK) which is a potent vasodilator by activating constitutive bradykinin B2- and inducible bradykinin B1 receptors-mediating nitric oxide and prostacyclin formation [7]. The PRCP-dependent BK generating pathway might be considered as an additional negative regulator of the pressor actions of the RAS.

In humans, PRCP has been recognized to have 2 mRNAs, termed as PRCP1 (Gene Bank NP_005131) and PRCP2 (NP_955450). The N-terminus of PRCP is where these isoforms diverge. There is no evidence suggesting whether PRCP2 mRNA encodes a functional protein.

PRCP is a polypeptide that folds back on itself to form a three-dimensional functional structure. The monomeric PRCP has the ability to undergo dimerization yet by an uncharcterized intramolecular mechanism of reaction. The residues involved in proteins dimerization differ from protein to protein. Generally, N-terminal, C-terminal, and transmembrane domains of a variety of proteins are found to be implicated in dimeric interaction [8–10]. The first 539 base pairs on the 5′-end of PRCP encode the putative transmembrane domain and the non-catalytic region [6]. PRCP1 had less than 30% similarity with the 3D structures of molecules found in the Protein Data Bank. Hence, it was difficult to guess the critical side chains. Therefore we focused on the functional importance of the N-terminal region of PRCP1 and test its role by site-directed mutagenesis, protein expression, and kinetic assessment.

The present investigation was designed to describe the expression and purification of human PRCP which does not contain the first 539 base pairs on the 5′-end (rPRCP539–1601). The rPRCP539–1601 contains the catalytic region and is highly conserved with human PRCP family of enzymes and with PRCP in other species. The rPRCP539–1601 is a N-terminal truncated form (ΔN179-PRCP), lacking 179 N-terminal residues of PRCP with an apparent molecular mass of 40 kDa. The 40 kDa recombinant human PRCP (rPRCP40) was characterized with respect to its biochemical and physical properties. Collectively, the metabolism of angiotensin molecules by rPRCP40 brings forth a new understanding into the mechanism of actions of PRCP, therefore allowing better insight into structure-function relationships.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Materials

Schneider insect (S2) cells were purchased from Invitrogen (Carlsbad, CA). Serum free insect cell growth medium was purchased from HyClone (Logan, UT). Diethylaminoethyl (DEAE) cellulose was purchased from Whatman (Fairfield, NJ). SP-Sephadex and all reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO). Angiotensin III, angiotensin 1–7, angiotensin I, H-Ala-Pro-pNA, and z-Pro-Pro-aldehyde-dimethyl acetate (Z-Pro-Prolinal) were purchased from Bachem (King of Prussia, PA). Angiotensin 2–7 was obtained from New England Peptide LLC (Gardner, MA). phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF) was obtained from Calbiochem (San Diego, CA).

### Expression and purification of wild-type and the mutant PRCP

In the past, the wild-type PRCP (rPRCP52) cDNAs has been incorporated into pMT/BIP/V5-HisC inducible/secreted expression vector and expressed in Schneider (S2) insect cells [11]. Therefore, we used the same strategy to clone and express a variant cDNA that deleted a sequence of 539 base pairs on 5′-terminal PRCP539–1607 cDNA into pMT/BiP/V5. The sense primer contained a 5′-encoding sequence (5′-GAA.TTT.CCT.GAC.ATC.AGA.ACA.AGC.TC -3′) and an EcoR I restriction site at the 5′ end. The antisense primer (3′-CCG.GAA.TTC.TCA.GTG.CTG.CTT.TCC.TGC.ACT -5′) had an EcoRI restriction site at the 3′ end. The EcoR I and EcoRI restriction sites were for direct cloning into the expression vector pMT/BiP/V5-His C (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA).

pMT/BiP-PRCP plasmid was expressed according to a previously described method [11]. The fidelity of the cDNA for PRCP was confirmed by DNA sequence analysis. The expressed wild-type (with a predicted molecular mass of about 52 kDa) and mutant PRCP (with a predicted molecular mass of 40 kDa) were separated by 10 % reduced SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (data not shown). The concentration of rPRCP was calculated by measuring its absorbance at 280 nm in a 1 cm pathlength cuvette using an UV-Vis spectrophotometer. The molar extinction coefficient was calculated to be 90,000 M−1cm−1. Using the Beer-Lambert Law, the concentration of protein was determined [12].

### Circular dichroism (CD) measurements

Far UV CD spectra and thermal-denaturation experiments were recorded on an AVIV 62D CD spectropolarimeter. Spectra in a 0.05 cm pathlength cuvette were at room temperature (22 °C) with 9.6 μM recombinant PRCP mutant in reaction buffer (0.01 M sodium acetate, 0.07 M potassium phosphate, and 1 mM EDTA pH 4.8). Spectra in a 1 cm pathlength cell were at 25 °C with 1 μM recombinant PRCP mutant protein in reaction buffer. Angiotensin III was added at 1 μM when present. Spectra were not background corrected. The thermal-denaturation experiments were performed in a 1 cm pathlength cell with a sealed top through which a temperature probe was inserted. Temperature was scanned from 15 to 85 °C while the CD signal was monitored at 225 nm. The concentration of recombinant PRCP mutant was at 1 μM in reaction buffer. Data are plotted against the probe temperature.

Data were analyzed using IGOR Pro (ver.4.0; Wavemetrics), with procedure files written in-house. Temperature induced unfolding transitions monitored by CD were fit to a two-state unfolding model represented as follows

$$ (1) Native ↔ Unfolded $$

The equilibrium constant, K, is given by

$$ (2) K = [ U ] [ N ] $$

The mole fraction of the unfolded species is given by

$$ (3) f U = K 1 + K ; K = e − Δ G R T $$

The relationship between free energy change and melting temperature is given by the equation shown below

(4) Δ G = Δ H m ( 1 − T T m ) + Δ C p ( T − T m − T · ln ( T T m ) ) where ΔHm is the enthalpy of unfolding at the melting temperature, Tm is the melting temperature and ΔCp is the heat capacity at the melting temperature [13]. Unfolding data from the CD were fit to Eq 3 and 4 with baseline slopes and intercepts as fitted parameters.

### Kinetic studies

The rate constants for PRCP substrate were determined for both the wild-type and purified mutant PRCPs in reaction buffer containing 0.01 M Na-acetate, 0.07 M potassium phosphate pH 5.8, at 37 °C. The slope of the initial linear increase in absorbance at 304 nm/min was used to determine PRCP activity. Blanks with substrate but no enzyme were run to verify that PRCP activity was measured as opposed to substrate auto-hydrolysis. The blank values were subtracted from those in the presence of enzyme to obtain enzyme catalyzed hydrolysis of the substrate. The Michaelis-Menten constant (Km, Vmax) were calculated from Lineweaver-Burke (1/S versus 1/V) plots and verified by Hanes-Woolf (S versus S/V) analysis.

### LC-MS Studies

LC-MS experiments for the analysis of angiotensin III and its metabolites were conducted based on the method of Cui [14], with modification. The instrumentation platform used consisted of a Waters Micromass ZQ single quadrupole mass spectrometer coupled to a Waters 2695 HPLC, controlled by Mass Lynx 4.0 Software. Peptide incubation mixtures were separated on a reverse-phase C18 column (Phenomenex Prodigy, 5 μm, ODS3, 100 × 4.6 mm) using a mobile phase consisting of water (spiked with 0.1% formic acid) and CH3CN at ambient temperature using a constant flow rate of 0.2 mL/min. The mobile phase gradient of 5% CH3CN in water was increased linearly to 20% CH3CN from 0 –10 minutes, to 50% CH3CN from 10–25 minutes, and decreased linearly to 5% CH3CN from 25–40 minutes. Electrospray ionization (ESI) parameters: capillary voltage, 3.2 kV; cone voltage, 15 V; extractor, 3V; desolvation temperature, 250 °C, desolvation gas flow, 400L/h, source temperature, 120 °C. LC-MS was performed using both TIC and SIR (single ion recording) mode. Angiotensin III (m/z 466.4 [MH]+2; Angiotensin III-Phe (m/z 392.9 [MH]+2). 10 μL of the incubation mixture containing AngIII and PRCP was diluted with water (240 μL) and 5 μL of this solution was used for analysis.

## RESULTS

### Structure and stability of recombinant PRC

The CD spectrum of rPRCP40 (Figure 1A) illustrates that it is structured with significant helical content as indicated by local minima at ~220 and 208 nm. Addition of equimolar levels of Ang III did not change the spectrum. Thermal denaturation of rPRCP40 is shown in (Figure 1B). The transition appears to be biphasic illustrating that unfolding occurs in a multistep process. Data were modeled as a simple 2-state transition (Eq 1) to provide estimates of the enthalpy of unfolding and melting temperature. Fits to Eq 2 and 3 resolved an enthalpy change upon unfolding of 33 ± 1 kcal/mol and Tm 35.3 ± 0.2 °C (ΔCp was fixed to 0 cal/molK). The enthalpy change resolved from a fit to a 2-state model less than the enthalpy for the individual fits to a 3 state transition. There was significant change in the CD spectrum after heating. Figure 1C shows a comparison of the spectra of PRCP with Ang III added to before and after a themal-denaturation experiment. These data suggest that the unfolding of rPRCP40 was irreversible even in the presence of Ang III.

To determine whether rPRCP40 behaved like native PRCP under steady-state kinetic conditions, we monitored the percent liberation of p-nitroanalide from Ala-Pro-para-nitroanalide over a range of temperature with a fixed time and enzyme concentration. The stability of rPRCP40 was tested by measuring Ala-Pro-pNA hydrolysis at various temperatures for 1 h. The activity of the rPRCP40 increased with assay temperature until the temperature reached 37°C. rPRCP40 activity gradually decreased at higher temperature, and became completely inactive, presumably by becoming denatured at temperatures above 60°C. These experiments along with thermal-denaturation experiments (Figure 1C) support the ideas that the N-terminal of PRCP may be involved in its structural stabilization.

### Kinetic characterization of rPRCP40

We next determined the kinetic parameters of rPRCP40. The specificity of rPRCP40 was studied by determining the kcat/Km values for the hydrolysis of Ala-Pro-pNA and angiotensin molecules substrates. Linearity of the reaction with time and amount of enzyme was determined in all experiments performed in this study. The rate of hydrolysis of Ala-Pro-pNA by rPRCP40 was plotted as a function of substrate concentration and is shown in (Figure 2). A hyperbolic dependence was observed for rPRCP40, consistent with Henri-Michaelis–Menten kinetics, using Ala-Pro-pNA. rPRCP40 like rPRCP52 as shown previously metabolized Ala-Pro-pNA in a dose- and time-dependent fashion (Figure 2A)[11]. The ratio of enzyme-to-chromogenic substrate was adjusted so that the rate of paranitroanalide release was linear over the course of the assay. The Km of rPRCP40 and of wild type rPRCP (rPRCP52) for Ala-Pro-pNA was 1.5 ± 0.4 mM and 3.1 ± 0.3 mM respectively. The catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) of the rPRCP40 protein towards Ala-Pro-pNA is 18.6 ± 3.4/sec. To demonstrate that Ala-Pro-pNA hydrolysis was not due to the activities of aminopeptidases and cathepsins, CdCl2 (3 mM), 1,10 phenanthroline (10 mM) and cystatin (1μM), inhibitors of aminopeptidases A and N, cathepsin B, H and L were added to the incubation cocktail. Our results suggested that the ability of rPRCP40 to hydrolyze the substrate was significantly improved in comparison to rPRCP52 (p ≤ 0.05) [11].

Recently, we showed that Ang II causes substrate inhibition of native endothelial PRCP and rPRCP52 [11;15]. To further characterize rPRCP40, substrate inhibition studies were performed. In the substrate inhibition studies, Ang III (a PRCP substrate), but not Ang1–7 (as control) inhibited rPRCP40 in a dose dependent manner suggesting the functional similarity of rPRCP40 with the native endothelial PRCP (Figure 2B) [[15]]. The effect of Ang II precursor, angiotensin I (Ang I) on rPRCP40 was determined. Ang I inhibited PRCP in a dose-dependent manner with an IC50 of 1 mM in the presence of 3 mM chromogenic substrate (Figure 2C).

For the first time, we developed a new and an accurate assay to determine PRCP catalytic activity. The reaction products from the conversion of Ang III, Ang 2–7, and Ang I by rPRCP40 were determined by LCMS. Reaction mixtures lacking enzyme served as negative controls, while rPRCP40 in the presence of the substrate was used as a positive control. As shown in (Figure 4A), rPRCP40 has the ability to convert Ang III (Arg2-Val3-125I-Tyr4-Ile5-His6-Pro7-Phe8) to Ang 2–7 (Arg2-Val3-125I-Tyr4-Ile5-His6-Pro7) and phenylalanine. Metabolism of Ang III (1 mM) by rPRCP40 (100 ng) resulted in three major peaks in comparison to the control (no enzyme) (Figure 3A). The unmetabolized amount of Ang III appeared at 31.58 min, whereas Ang 2–7 and phenylalanine appeared at 28.33 and 26.11 min respectively. Unmetabolized fraction of Ang III by rPRCP40 had a similar retention time as the control (Ang III alone) (Figure 3 A (inset)). This is a novel finding because N-terminally truncated PRCP like that of endothelial PRCP, which is known for its ability to cleave Pro-X bonds to release the C-terminal amino acid [16], can generate identical metabolites (Ang 2–7 and phenylalanine). To determine the generation of potential secondary metabolites, Ang 2–7 or Ang 1–7 were incubated with rPRCP40. No secondary metabolites were formed by rPRCP40 (Figure 3B) in comparison to the control (Figure 4B inset). Similarly, no secondary metabolites were formed when rPRCP40 was incubated with Ang1–7 (Figure 3C). Ang 1–7 in the absence of rPRCP40 was used as a negative control (Figure 4C inset). The incubation of rPRCP40 with Ang I (an ACE 2 substrate) resulted in no metabolite generation (Figure 3D). Ang III was used as a standard and shown in (Figure 3E). When a combination of Ang I (1mM) and Ang III (1 mM) were incubated with rPRCP40, it resulted in the generation of Ang 2–7. However, the level of Ang 2–7 generated by rPRCP40 in the presence of Ang I was significantly reduced, suggesting that Ang I might be the endogenous inhibitor of PRCP (Figure 3F). These data suggested that the main products of Ang III or Ang II metabolized by rPRCP40 are Ang 2–7 and phenylalanine or Ang 1–7 and phenylalanine respectively.

## DISCUSSION

In view of the role of PRCP in RAS and KKS pathways, investigations were performed to characterize molecular structure and function analysis of recombinant PRCP on the metabolism of Ang III and Ang II. To our surprise, the enzymatic properties of rPRCP40 and mature rPRCP52 characterized in the present investigation indicate that the two proteins have similar functional activities on Ang II and Ang III.

rPRCP40 was tested for its ability to metabolize Ala-Pro-pNA, as well as Ang II and Ang III. The affinity for Ala-Pro-pNA for rPRCP40 was higher than for the wild type enzyme. The hydrolysis of substrate by rPRCP40 followed Michaelis-Menten kinetics with the KM value decreased by a factor of two when compared with the wild type. The catalytic efficiency of rPRCP40 was approximately two-fold higher than the wild type. In substrate inhibition studies, Ang III but not Ang 1–7 in increasing concentration blocked Ala-Pro-pNA hydrolysis. Angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE 2) forms angiotensin 1–9 from angiotensin 1 (Ang 1). Ang I blocked both Ala-Pro-pNA metabolism (Figure 2 C) and Ang III metabolism (Figure 2 F), suggesting that it may be an endogenous inhibitor of PRCP.

The most prominent effect caused by extended incubation of Ang III with PRCP is a near total inactivation of Ang III which eliminates its ability to cause AT1 receptor stimulation (Figure 3A). PRCP converted Ang III to Ang 2–7 with no other metabolites being observed.

The temperature inactivation and inhibition studies confirmed the uniqueness of the rPRCP40’s function. rPRCP40 was found to be much less stable upon incubation at temperatures higher than 50 °C than endothelial PRCP as was observed earlier, [16;17]. This finding could only be due to folding nature of recombinant PRCP.

Efficient conversion of Ang II to Ang 1–7 by ACE2 as well as PRCP and Ang III to Ang 2–7 by PRCP are critical on endothelium that are continuously exposed to a variety of vasopressor molecules. Therefore, vasodilation rather than vasoconstriction pathways are favored, sustaining function and preparing endothelium to receive the next wave of vasoconstrictor stimuli. PRCP activity provides a measure of endothelium relaxation capacity due to its ability to initiate nitric oxide and prostaglandin generation via kallikrein generation [7;15]. ACE2 and PRCP are gauges of endothelium relaxation processes.

PRCP is a homodimer and the biochemical and physical nature of this dimerization is not known. It is tempting to speculate that the first 179 residues of N-terminal region of PRCP, which is lacking in rPRCP40 could play an important role in the folding and the dimerization of the polypeptides. Our observation that β-mercaptoethanol does not reduce substrate hydrolysis indicates that cysteine oxidation may not be involved in rPRCP40-induced substrate hydrolysis. The inability of β-mercaptoethanol or DTT to inactivate rPRCP40 has several implications. First, the PRCP monomer containing the catalytic domain retains the ability to metabolize Ang III and Ala-Pro-pNA. Secondly, dimers of PRCP could be the inactive form. Identification and characterization of yet another unidentified modulator that might regulate the equilibrium between the active monomer and the inactive dimers of PRCP will require further investigations.

In conclusion, the structural basis of how PRCP can bind and selectively metabolize a variety of different peptides and protein is far from clear. The work presented here is the first description of the role of N-terminal region of PRCP in the production of Ang 1–7 and Ang 2–7 using LC-MS. It is also the first demonstration of an instance in which Ang I blocks the conversion of Ang III to Ang 2–7 by PRCP. The data thus suggest that a selective increase in Ang I in plasma may be helpful to prevent hypotensive effects of Ang 1–7, Ang 2–7, and bradykinin through PRCP-mediated PK activation. Despite the incomplete characterization of PRCP, we showed that the C-terminal region of the rPRCP40 contributes to PRCP’s catalytic function, and provided additional experimental evidence for this suggestion.

## ABSTRACT

RYAN C. PERKINS: Characterization of the Lipopolysaccharide Binding Site on the Plasma Protein High Molecular Weight Kininogen

Bradykinin (BK) participates in the control of local blood flow and blood pressure by

causing vascular hyperemia and vascular inflammation. The Bradykinin generating

pathway of human plasma consists of prolylcarboxypeptidase (PRCP), prekallikrein

(PK), and high molecular weight kininogen (HK). When the complex of HK-PK

assembles on endothelial cells or an artificial negatively charged surface, PK is

immediately converted to kallikrein by the enzyme PRCP. The formed kallikrein then

autodigests HK to liberate BK. The BK that is formed then plays an important role in

vascular permeability by stimulating constitutive Bradykinin B2 and inducible B1

receptors to release prostacyclin and nitric oxide. Thus, the activity of PRCP leads to

vasodilation. In inflamed tissues, tissue injury or hypotensive bacteremia, BK has been

shown to accumulate in the blood or plasma of patients. Since LPS possesses a

negatively charged surface and the ability to stimulate an inflammatory response, the

interaction of LPS with the proteins of the Bradykinin generating pathway assessed and

characterized. These studies showed that the binding of LPS to HK was time dependent,

dose dependent, saturable and reversible. The binding of LPS to HK was shown to occur

via the positively charged amino acid residues of domain 5 interacting with the

negatively charged moieties of LPS. The binding of LPS to HK was further shown to be

maximal at pH 7.0 and in an isotonic environment. The binding of LPS to HK was

D. Nitric Oxide

Nitric Oxide (NO) is a two-atom compound that is synthesized physiologically by

various tissue and cell types in the body and plays a complex role in physiology. In the

cardiovascular system, NO acts as a mediator of vasodilation in the endothelium helping

to regulate vessel tone, but also plays a role in the regulation of platelet aggregation,

leukocyte adhesion, paracrine and autocrine pathways involving control of vascular cell

growth and remodeling, endothelial cell apoptosis, migration and organization. NO

synthesis from L-arginine in endothelial cells is catalyzed by the enzyme Nitric Oxide

Synthase (eNOS). Studies have shown that physiologically eNOS is activated by

increasing the levels of intracellular calcium present. The increasing calcium levels will

in turn upregulate the binding of calmodulin to eNOS. eNOS, a transmembrane protein,

is found on Golgi and caveolar membranes; however, the targeting of eNOS to caveolae

is dependent upon co- and post-translational modification (myristoylation,

palmitoylation) which are required for optimal enzymatic activity.^

E. Renin-Angiotensin System

The Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS), similar to Bradykinin, plays an important

role in the regulation of blood pressure and the vascular response to injury. This

relationship can be illustrated due to the dual roles of RAS in the homeostasis of salt and

water in the body’s response to vascular injury. Damage to the endothelial wall can be

caused due to the increased mechanical strain that is associated with high blood pressure.

When RAS is activated, the blood pressure is increased which leads to the causation of a

local inflammatory response to aid in repairing the injury. Due to elevated blood

leads to microvascular damage and endothelial dysfunction. This response has

pathophysiological effects increasing the chances of myocardial infarction, heart failure.

11 stroke, peripheral arterial disease, and renal disease.

The Renin Angiotensin System plays an important role in protecting the heart,

endothelium, brain and kidney from sustained exposure to blood pressures that exceeds

the physiological range through a complex system of neuroendocrine interactions.

Continual activation of RAS results in the causation of hypertension and activates a

cascade of proinflammatory, prothrombotic and atherogenic effects. The synthesis of the

central metabolite Ang I is largely dependent upon the activity of renin. Renin, an

enzymatic hormone that plays an important role in salt regulation by the kidneys, is

synthesized and released by the liver to counter act decreases in renal perfusion pressure.

This released renin then catalyzes the conversion of angiotensinogen into the inactive

peptide Angiotensin I (Ang I, Asp-Arg-Val-Tyr-Ile-His-Pro-Phe-His-Leu). As the

central metabolite of RAS, Ang I can then follow three different paths. Ang I can be

converted into the vasoactive peptide Ang II (Asp-Arg-Val-Tyr-He-His-Pro-Phe) by

angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). In this conversion, ACE cleaves the His-Leu

residues from the carboxy terminus of the peptide. Surprisingly, not all of the conversion

from Ang I to Ang II is done by ACE. In fact, nearly ~ 40% of the conversion is

catalyzed through chymase, cathepsin G, and other serine proteases. The formed Ang II

is then known to interact with at least 2 different receptors, angiotensin II receptor

subtype 1 (ATi) and angiotensin II receptor subtype 2 (AT2). Of the two Ang II receptor

subtypes, the AT 1 receptor has been more readily characterized and is understood in

contributes to the proinflammatory, atherogenic, and prothrombotic environment. The

binding of Ang II to ATi receptors can be blocked by the ATi antagonist, angiotensin

IV. DISCUSSION

Since PK can only be converted to Kallikrein when HK is bound to the cell

membrane surface or an artificial negative surface and LPS possesses a negatively

charged domain with the ability to induce an inflammatory response in humans, the

interaction of LPS and HK was determined. In this study we show that the binding of

LPS to HK occurs in a time dependent, dose dependent, saturable and reversible manner.

The interaction of LPS on HK was shown to occur via the positively charged

Lysine residues on domain 5. Furthermore, this interaction can be inhibited by HKH19,

diethyl pyrocarbonated HKH19, and heparin. In addition, this study shows that the HK

binding site on LPS is the polysaccharide chain. Inhibition of this interaction occurred by

A^-acetylglucosamine glycan and C1-Inhibitor. These data reveal that LPS binds to HK

and this interaction possesses insights that might potentially be utilized in treating

patients with hypotensive bactermia and sepsis.

In order to further characterize this interaction, a set of competitive inhibition

studies were undertaken based on the prior data that was collected. Our data suggests

that the attraction of C1 -Inhibitor for LPS outcompetes the binding of LPS to HK. It is

reasonable to speculate that this interaction of Cl-Inhibitor with LPS might lead to the

continual amassing of Kallikrein and activated FXII during endotoximea. In addition, the

ability of heparin to inhibit LPS binding to HK was not affected in the presence or

absence of physiological concentration of HK (600 nM). This data could be applicable to

34


<!-- Page 43 -->


future studies to determine if HK is involved in the removal of free heparin from

systemic circulation in patients suffering from sepsis.

The activation of the Kallikrein Kinin System plays an important role in hypertension and

inflammation. Therefore, the KKS metabolites play an integral role in health and disease.

Since the KKS system is responsible for the production of BK and HKa, our data

emphasizes the importance of HK, BK, and HKa in infection. However, further

investigations need to be undertaken in order to characterize its predictive values in

inflammation.

Furthermore, our data further provides evidence that HK plays a protective role in

the coagulation system against infection. Our interesting and novel method of

characterizing the inhibition of microbial binding (via HKH19, heparin, and Cl-inhibitor)

to the cell surface, should be further investigated with clinical studies, as it possesses

potential therapeutic implications for patients with sepsis and hypotensive bactermia.

## Abstract

## Background

Migrant and ethnic minority populations participate in organised colorectal cancer (CRC) screening

programmes at consistently lower rates than host populations across high-income countries. Prior

qualitative research has identified barriers spanning cultural beliefs, health literacy, and system access,

but these have predominantly been examined as discrete, domain-specific factors, with little focus on

how these barriers co-occur and interact. First-generation Middle Eastern migrants are particularly underscreened and remain largely absent from qualitative research on screening engagement. This study

explored factors influencing CRC screening participation among first-generation Middle Eastern

migrants in Australia, using inductive thematic analysis to examine how barriers are experienced within

this community.

## Methods

A qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with nineteen first-generation Middle Eastern

migrants aged 50–74 years, eligible for Australia’s National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (NBCSP),

was conducted in New South Wales between August 2023 and August 2024. Participants were recruited through community organisations. Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis following Braun

and Clarke, supplemented by participant-level barrier matrix mapping.

## Results

Of the 19 participants: 12 had never completed screening, 5 had completed at least one kit but not their

most recent, and 2 completed their screening consistently. Despite high rates of non-participation, most

reported openness to future screening. Four themes shaped participation: psycho-socio-cultural

attitudes towards cancer and risk; socially mediated health information and trust; health system access and engagement; and modality-specific barriers related to the faecal immunochemical test (FIT)

process. Barriers co-occurred and interacted across domains within individual accounts, and barrier

configurations varied markedly across participants: no two participants presented the same barrier

combination. Screening readiness was context-dependent, with cycles of intention and deferral shaped

by life circumstances and programme timing.

## Conclusions

Our findings show that barriers to colorectal cancer screening among first-generation Middle Eastern migrants co-occur, differ across individuals, and shift over time. This heterogeneity argues against

uniform targeted interventions and for an adaptive screening architecture – flexible in modality, timing,

## Background

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most commonly diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of

cancer-related death worldwide [1]. Early detection through population-based screening substantially

improves survival: five-year relative survival approaches 99% for localised disease but falls below 15%

for advanced stages [2, 3]. Organised screening programmes using faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) have been implemented across high-income countries, including Australia, the United Kingdom, the

Netherlands, and several other European nations, with participation targets typically set between 65%

and 80% to maximise population benefit [4–7].

Despite established programme infrastructure, participation remains unevenly distributed. Migrant and

ethnic minority populations consistently screen at lower rates than host populations across multiple

national programmes [8–10]. In Australia, where the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (NBCSP)

has offered biennial FIT to adults aged 50–74 years through a home-based postal model - with eligibility

extended from 1 July 2024 to allow adults aged 45–49 to request their first kit - overall participation was 41.7% in 2022–2023 [11, 12], well below the national target, and is significantly lower among culturally

and linguistically diverse migrant communities [13–15]. Within these communities, first-generation

Middle Eastern migrants represent a particularly under-screened group [14, 16–19] yet remain largely

absent from qualitative research on screening engagement [20, 21].

A substantial body of qualitative research has examined barriers to CRC screening among migrant and

ethnic minority populations internationally, identifying important factors such as limited health literacy,

symptom-led risk appraisal, cancer fatalism and stigma, reliance on clinician endorsement, and

modality-specific aversions [8, 22–28]. These barriers have typically been organised into discrete domains – cultural beliefs, health system access, individual psycho-social factors – and treated as

independent factors amenable to separate interventions [24, 29]. Less attention has been given to how

barriers interact or co-occur within individual experience, how the profile of barriers varies across

individuals within the same community, or whether screening readiness is stable or responsive to

changing life circumstances [30, 31]. These questions have direct implications for intervention design: if

barrier experience is heterogeneous within a community rather than shared across it, then the

expectation that identifying barriers within a defined population enables the design of uniform targeted interventions may itself warrant examination [17, 30, 32].

This study explored factors influencing CRC screening participation among first-generation Middle Eastern migrants in Australia. Australia’s NBCSP - a nationally organised, FIT-based programme delivered

through a home-based postal model on a fixed biennial schedule [11, 31, 33] - exemplifies the uniform screening delivery architecture common to organised programmes internationally. Using inductive thematic analysis, we examined what barriers and influences participants reported, and how these were

Page 3/33


<!-- Page 4 -->


experienced and configured within individual accounts. The findings suggest that closing participation disparities cannot be addressed solely through improved outreach within the existing delivery model.

Instead, we propose an adaptive screening architecture: a delivery strategy in which core programme components - modality, timing, engagement channel, and educational framing - are combined and adjusted to accommodate individual barrier configurations. We position this as a shift from equality of

offering toward equity of opportunity.

## Methods

## Study design

We conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and inductive thematic analysis [34],

informed by a pragmatic, applied qualitative orientation. The study aimed to identify participant-reported influences on CRC screening engagement without applying a pre-specified explanatory framework.

## Setting and context

The study was conducted in New South Wales, Australia, between August 2023 and August 2024 within the context of Australia’s publicly funded NBCSP. During most of the study period, the NBCSP offered biennial FIT screening to adults aged 50–74 years through a home-based postal model, with kits

completed independently and returned by post without direct clinical involvement. From 1 July 2024, the starting age for the programme was lowered to 45 years; adults aged 45–49 years could request their

first FIT kit, while adults aged 50–74 years continued to receive kits biennially through the mail [11]. Participants were recruited through Sydney-based cultural and religious community organisations

serving Middle Eastern migrant communities.

## Participants and recruitment

Eligible participants were aged 50–74 years at study commencement, born overseas, self-identified as

Middle Eastern, able to communicate in English, and willing to participate in an online interview. Eligibility criteria reflected the NBCSP age range in effect at the time of study commencement; the subsequent

lowering of the starting age to 45 years (from 1 July 2024) did not alter the recruitment criteria. Recruitment was conducted on a rolling basis through posters displayed at participating Sydney-based cultural and religious community organisations. Interested individuals contacted the research team

directly using the details provided on the study materials. All eligible volunteers who responded were included. Written informed consent was obtained before participation.

Nineteen participants were recruited, with variation in age, sex, country of birth, screening history, and length of residence in Australia. Recruitment and analysis proceeded iteratively rather than to a

predetermined sample size. Sample size was guided by the concept of information power, which

Page 4/33


<!-- Page 5 -->


considers the study aim, sample specificity, quality of dialogue, and analytic strategy [35]. Several factors supported adequacy at this sample size: the study aim was narrow and applied; the sample was highly

specific to the target population; interviews achieved substantial dialogue quality, with most lasting 40 minutes or longer and generating detailed accounts of screening decision-making; and the inductive analytic strategy drew on cross-case comparison rather than requiring saturation of a pre-specified

theoretical framework [35]. The research team judged that 19 interviews provided sufficient informational richness and thematic depth to address the study aims. No participants declined or

withdrew from the study.

## Data collection

Interviews were conducted by the first author, a male MD/PhD candidate of Middle Eastern background

with formal qualitative research training in interview-based methods and thematic analysis, and no prior relationship with participants. A semi-structured interview guide (Supplementary file 1) was developed

from relevant literature and expert consultation and explored views and experiences relating to bowel cancer screening, health service engagement, and interactions with the NBCSP invitation and FIT kit

process. Two early interviews were used to pilot the guide; no substantive changes were made, and these interviews were retained in the final analysis.

One-to-one interviews were conducted in English via online video call and ranged from 20 to 70 minutes

(mean 40 minutes). No non-participants were present during interviews, and repeat interviews were not conducted. Although the guide was used consistently across interviews, participants were able to

elaborate on issues they considered important before returning to the core topics. Audio recordings were transcribed verbatim using OpenAI Whisper (V2) [36] and manually checked against the recordings for

accuracy. Participants received a copy of their transcript within five days for factual review; no substantive amendments were requested. The analytic record comprised audio recordings, verified transcripts, and ongoing analytic discussion. No formal observational field notes were recorded.

## Data analysis

Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke [34]. Transcripts were managed in Microsoft Word and Excel, and analysis began alongside data collection and proceeded

iteratively. Two researchers coded all transcripts in parallel using open coding to identify barriers, influences, and decision-making factors related to screening participation described in participants’

accounts. After the first eight to ten interviews, an initial working coding framework was developed and then iteratively refined as subsequent transcripts were analysed. Candidate subthemes and broader themes were generated through comparison and grouping of codes across transcripts and were refined

through team discussion. Divergent interpretations were explored through discussion and joint rereading of transcripts, with the aim of refining and deepening interpretation rather than establishing

formal coding agreement. No inter-coder reliability statistics were calculated. Later interviews yielded refinements to existing subthemes, but no substantively new barrier concepts or thematic domains

Page 5/33


<!-- Page 6 -->


emerged, supporting the judgement that the sample provided sufficient thematic depth for the study aims.

After development of the final themes, subthemes, and barrier concepts, we undertook a secondary

participant-level matrix mapping step to examine how specific barriers were distributed across the sample. Matrix rows represented participants and columns represented individual barrier concepts

derived from the final coding framework. For each participant, a barrier was coded as present when the transcript contained either an explicit statement or a clear contextual account indicating that the barrier

contributed to non-participation, delay, reluctance, or difficulty engaging with screening. Repeated references to the same barrier within a participant’s interview were counted once at participant level

only. Matrix coding used binary presence/absence values and was based on the participant’s account as a whole rather than isolated quotations. Initial matrix mapping was undertaken by the first author and reviewed by a second researcher against the original transcripts to ensure that barrier assignment

remained grounded in the full narrative context; uncertainties were resolved through discussion and return to transcript context. The matrix was used descriptively to examine participant-level heterogeneity,

summarise the distribution and frequency of barriers across the sample, and identify where barriers from different thematic domains co-occurred within the same participant account. Absence of a barrier in the

matrix indicates that it was not identified in that participant’s interview rather than definitive absence from that participant’s lived experience. Co-occurrence was treated as an analytic aid for interpretation

rather than as evidence of statistical association or causal interaction.

In addition, close reading of participants’ retrospective accounts was used to examine how reported openness to screening shifted according to explanation, circumstances, and timing. These temporal

interpretations were derived from narrative reading of participant accounts rather than from matrix mapping. Researcher reflexivity and rigour

The interviewer’s shared Middle Eastern background was a deliberate methodological consideration

intended to facilitate trust and disclosure on culturally sensitive topics, including cancer stigma, fatalism, and aversion to stool handling. At the same time, cultural proximity carried a risk of assumed shared understanding and under-probing of responses that appeared self-evident. To mitigate this, the interviewer used reflective prompts during interviews to encourage participants to elaborate on meanings and experiences that might otherwise have remained implicit. A second clinician-researcher,

who was also a first-generation migrant to Australia, of South Asian background, contributed an additional analytic perspective during coding and interpretation, while maintaining sensitivity to migration and cultural context.

A key reflexive observation concerned the team’s prior assumptions about the data. The research team initially anticipated finding a relatively shared set of barriers experienced within this participant group, expecting that individuals from the same cultural background would describe similar barriers to screening. This expectation was progressively challenged during analysis as significant within-group

Page 6/33


<!-- Page 7 -->


variation became apparent and emerged as an explicit focus of interpretation, resulting in the formation of the participant-level barrier matrix map.

Analytic rigour was supported through iterative recruitment and analysis, parallel coding followed by collaborative interpretation, and maintenance of an audit trail linking transcript excerpts to codes,

subthemes, themes, and participant-level matrix mapping. Participants were invited to review transcripts for factual accuracy but were not asked to comment on the analytic interpretation. Detailed reporting of participant characteristics and study context was provided to support assessment of transferability. Reporting followed the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist [37]

(Supplementary file 2).

## Discussion

This study explored factors influencing CRC screening participation among first-generation Middle Eastern migrants in Australia, a population that screens at substantially lower rates than both the general

population and other migrant groups [8, 14, 16, 17], yet remains largely absent from qualitative research

on screening engagement. The individual barriers reported here (symptom-led risk appraisal, cancer fatalism and stigma, reliance on clinician endorsement, stool handling aversion, and competing life

pressures) are well documented across migrant and ethnic minority populations internationally [8, 22–

28, 32, 38]. The contribution of this study lies in three observations about how barriers configure within and across individuals, and shift over time (Fig. 2): (1) the specific combination of barriers shaping an

individual’s non-participation - what we term their barrier configuration - varied markedly across individuals within a single cultural sub-group; (2) barriers consistently co-occurred across thematic

domains within individual accounts; and (3) screening readiness was described as context-dependent

and episodic rather than stable.

## Barrier configurations varied across individuals within the same community

The participant-barrier matrix revealed substantial variation in barrier profiles across the sample. Participants differed in how many barriers they reported, which thematic domains featured in their

accounts, and the conditions under which screening would become actionable. This variation was

present within a demographically narrow sample in which participants shared a common cultural background, were predominantly from a single country of origin, resided in the same city, and were

eligible for the same screening programme. While no two participants presented the same barrier combination, the heterogeneity observed was not simply a function of combinatorial possibility across

24 binary barrier concepts; it was evident in the range of barrier burden, from single-domain profiles to

dense configurations spanning all four themes, and in the qualitatively distinct circumstances under which participants described screening as actionable.

Two cases illustrate the programmatic relevance of this variation. One participant (P6) expressed willingness to be screened readily if a blood test integrated into routine pathology were available but

would not complete the FIT kit under any circumstances. By contrast, another participant (P2) who had completed the FIT previously with no modality-related difficulty described their barrier as entirely

temporal. These represent qualitatively different barrier configurations that would require different

programmatic responses, and they cannot be resolved by a single intervention targeting the most prevalent barrier in the group.

This heterogeneity challenges a common assumption in the screening disparities literature: that identifying barriers within a defined population enables the design of targeted interventions for that

group [8, 29, 30, 39]. Treating a migrant community as homogeneous in its screening barriers may obscure individual variation shaped by distinct migration histories, health system encounters, and

personal dispositions [30, 31]. If heterogeneity of this magnitude were present within our narrow sample,

it is reasonable to expect at least comparable variation within broader and more diverse migrant populations. The relevant question may therefore be less “what barriers does this community face?” than

“how do those barriers combine differently across individuals, and what does that variation mean for intervention design?” Barriers co-occurred across domains and were described as interacting

Among the 12 participants who had never screened, only one (P3) had barriers confined to a single thematic domain. For the remaining 11, screening non-participation reflected barriers operating

simultaneously across psycho-socio-cultural, informational, health system, and modality-specific

domains. Addressing a barrier in one domain while leaving others intact may therefore be insufficient to shift the outcome: improving kit instructions, for example, would not resolve stool handling aversion or

fear of diagnosis operating together within the same individual’s account [32, 40].

Several participants described co-occurring barriers not merely as coexisting but as interacting and

compounding one another. For P10, low perceived need made it easier to defer screening, and the kit then failed at the point of attempted use. For P6, time pressure and the multi-step process burden were

described as tightly connected, producing repeated postponement rather than a single decision not to

screen. Whether these interactions operate through specific causal mechanisms cannot be established from qualitative data and would require investigation beyond the scope of this study. However, the

## Screening readiness shifted with circumstances and timing

Many participants described their readiness to screen as context-dependent and episodic, rather than a

stable disposition. Repeated cycles of intention and deferral were common: the FIT kit entered the home, was set aside under competing pressures, and expired or was discarded without clinical follow-up. For

some, readiness was reactivated by a triggering event such as a friend’s diagnosis, only to be displaced again by competing demands.

This pattern was illustrated by the five participants with incomplete screening participation, each of whom had completed at least one FIT in a previous round but chose not to participate in their most

recent screening kit invitation. Renewed disengagement was driven by a reduced perceived urgency

following a prior negative result, competing life demands, and dissatisfaction with the stool-based process. P12’s account was distinct: she described willingness to screen and had no barriers identified

in her account, but missed the most recent round because she was moving house when the kit arrived

and had no prompt from the programme to re-engage once her circumstances changed. Prior completion did not establish ongoing engagement; repeat-round participation remained vulnerable both

to context-dependent shifts in readiness and to purely logistical disruptions that the fixed-schedule model could not accommodate.

The NBCSP, like most organised screening programmes, delivers a single invitation on a fixed schedule with a finite completion window [11]. If an individual’s readiness does not coincide with that window, the

opportunity passes, and the programme has no mechanism to re-engage at the moment readiness

returns [19, 43]. Participants’ accounts suggest that the consequence is not permanent refusal but a structural mismatch: people who described willingness to screen under the right circumstances did not

screen because the programme was not available when they were ready. These observations are drawn from retrospective accounts rather than longitudinal observation, and whether readiness fluctuates in

the manner described would require prospective investigation across multiple screening rounds to

establish. The distinction between barriers shaping first-time non-participation and those driving repeatround disengagement has received limited attention in the screening literature and warrants dedicated

investigation [19, 23, 43, 44].

## Implications for screening programme design: From uniform delivery to an adaptive screening architecture

Together, these findings suggest that the persistence of screening inequities among migrant populations

may not only reflect a failure of communication or outreach but a limitation of the uniform delivery model itself. Current efforts to address disparities have focused on two broad strategies. The first

targets the message: adapting communication through multilingual materials, community outreach, and

translated instructions, while leaving the delivery pathway unchanged [15, 33, 45]. The second, increasingly framed as precision screening, targets the recipient: using individual risk profiles to calibrate

when and how intensively a person should be screened [46]. Both strategies represent important advances. However, neither addresses a problem that our findings foreground: even with an accurately

stratified risk profile and a perfectly communicated invitation, an individual who faces a specific

configuration of co-occurring barriers across multiple domains may still be unable to engage with the screening pathway as delivered [30, 31].

We propose the concept of an adaptive screening architecture: a delivery strategy in which the core components of a screening programme - modality, timing, engagement channel, and educational framing

- are not fixed but can be combined and adjusted to accommodate individual barrier configurations. Precision screening identifies the right people to screen by stratifying risk based on demographic,

clinical, genetic, behavioural, or biological factors [46]. An adaptive screening architecture addresses

how to reach them, by adapting delivery to the barriers, readiness, access constraints, and life circumstances that determine whether eligible individuals actually participate [30, 31]. The goal is equity

of opportunity rather than equality of offering: ensuring that differences in modality preference, timing constraints, language, and health literacy do not determine whether an individual engages with

screening, so that the decision of whether to screen reflects individual choice rather than a structural

mismatch (Fig. 3).

The principle that screening delivery should adapt to the individual is already gaining traction at the level

of modality. The American Cancer Society’s 2026 updated guideline now includes blood-based CRC screening as a non-preferred option for individuals who decline or do not complete preferred stool-based

testing or colonoscopy, reflecting the pragmatic principle that the most diagnostically preferred test may

not be the most effective option for a person who will not complete it. [47]. Our findings suggest that this same logic extends beyond modality to every component of the delivery pathway. For participants in this

study, barriers were not confined to the test itself: they spanned informational access, trust, timing, competing demands, and the engagement channel through which the invitation arrived. An adaptive

architecture would therefore need to operate across these dimensions simultaneously - for example,

embedding a screening prompt within a chronic disease review for someone who will not act on a postal invitation, or re-engaging at the moment readiness returns rather than waiting for the next fixed cycle [26,

48–50]. Individually, any one of these adaptations is unlikely to substantially shift participation, precisely because barrier configurations are individually composed: addressing modality alone will not resolve the

barriers of someone whose non-participation is shaped by fear, competing demands, and absent GP endorsement [30, 32]. The defining feature of an adaptive architecture is the capacity to combine

adaptations in response to individual needs [48].

The participants in this study were not disengaged from healthcare; most were actively accessing

primary care and managing ongoing health concerns. Their non-participation was specific to screening. An adaptive strategy is designed for precisely this profile: individuals who are reachable within the health

system but for whom the fixed screening pathway does not align with their circumstances [48]. For those

not engaging with the health system at all, adaptive programme delivery alone would be insufficient without other strategies to facilitate health system contact.

Any move towards adaptive screening delivery would need to be designed with equity safeguards. Realising such a strategy at population scale would require digital infrastructure capable of integrating

individual-level data across primary care, pathology, and screening programmes - an implementation challenge that warrants dedicated investigation alongside questions of feasibility, equity implications,

and effectiveness across diverse programme contexts [48, 51]. The populations most in need of

adaptive pathways are often those least represented in the data systems that would inform them [51, 52].

## Strengths and limitations

## Sample and study design

This study contributes in-depth qualitative evidence from an under-studied population, with detailed data

on how barriers co-occur across thematic domains, vary across individuals within the same community, and shift with life circumstances over time. The interviewer’s shared Middle Eastern background may

have facilitated disclosure on culturally sensitive topics including cancer stigma, fatalism, and stool

handling aversion.

Participants were recruited through community organisations in New South Wales and were required to communicate in English, potentially excluding individuals for whom language itself constitutes a major

barrier. The sample was predominantly Lebanese, and barrier configurations may differ among other

Middle Eastern sub-groups. The recruitment strategy relied on posters displayed at community settings and did not restrict participation based on healthcare engagement. However, individuals fully disengaged

from these community settings or who are disengaged with healthcare are less likely to encounter

recruitment materials or self-select into interview-based health research. Reflecting this, most participants in our sample were actively engaged with primary care while not participating in screening.

Findings should therefore be interpreted with recognition that the experiences of those fully disengaged from the healthcare system may be underrepresented.

As a qualitative study with 19 participants, findings are not intended to be statistically representative and transferability to other contexts requires empirical investigation. Self-reported screening history was not

verified against programme records. The temporal dimension of barrier operation was derived from

retrospective accounts in cross-sectional interviews rather than from longitudinal observation and should be interpreted accordingly. Participant-barrier matrix

The participant-barrier matrix provided a structured empirical basis for the co-occurrence and

heterogeneity observations that extends beyond narrative description alone. This approach may be transferable to other screening contexts where within-group variation warrants examination. However,

binary presence/absence coding does not capture the relative importance or severity of each barrier for a given individual. Co-occurrence in the matrix indicates that barriers were present within the same

participant’s account but does not establish that they interacted causally; the linked narratives described

in the discussion are interpretive and would require future mixed-methods or longitudinal investigation to confirm. The matrix also reflects what participants reported during a single interview - barriers not raised

are recorded as absent rather than definitively not experienced. The extent to which these patterns hold across other communities, screening modalities, and national programme contexts - and whether

adaptive screening architectures can feasibly accommodate them - are questions for future research.

## Conclusions

Among first-generation Middle Eastern migrants in Australia, screening non-participation reflected

individually configured barrier combinations that co-occurred across domains, varied markedly across individuals, and shifted with circumstances over time. These patterns suggest that variation within

communities may be as consequential for screening programme design as variation between them, and

that pursuing equity of opportunity rather than equality of offering may require moving beyond the

uniform delivery model toward an adaptive screening architecture - one capable of accommodating

individual barrier configurations through flexibility in modality, timing, engagement, and educational framing pathways. Whether such architectures can be equitably implemented at population scale to

reduce participation disparities remains an open question warranting investigation across diverse

programme contexts.
